deliverable.title: Battlecard — Small Door Veterinary
deliverable.subject_label: Thicket vs. Digitail — for Small Door Veterinary

sentences.text: Small Door runs sixteen clinics across Boston, New York and Washington DC, and its public promise is availability — same or next-day appointments, and exams that start on time.
That makes scheduling a marketing problem for them rather than an IT problem, and it is the frame to open with.
Digitail sells the opposite motion: replace the whole practice-management stack with one AI-native platform.
Thicket's line here is that we make the calendar they already have work harder — not that they should rip out their PIMS.
Thicket Practice is $18 per seat per month with a three-seat minimum; Digitail publishes no price at all — every plan on their pricing page routes to a demo or to sales.
Their integrated phone system and mass texting are listed as add-ons rather than included in a plan.
Do not claim to be cheaper. We have no number for their plan, and a confident wrong number on a live call is how this deal is lost.
Digitail does include unlimited staff users at no additional cost, which is a genuine advantage over per-seat pricing once a practice has sixteen front desks.
Thicket writes bookings back to Digitail, ezyVet and Cornerstone within sixty seconds, so a practice keeps the system its staff already trained on.
Our median go-live for a four-location practice is nine days; Digitail's own page says most clinics go live in weeks, not months.
Our pricing is published and theirs is not — and for a practice that markets No Surprise Bills. Ever. to its own clients, that contrast is worth naming out loud.
Thicket is the only scheduling tool that writes back to all three major veterinary PIMS.
Digitail is an all-in-one practice management system. Thicket does scheduling and client communication only — no medical records, no invoicing, no inventory.
If Small Door is already unhappy with its current PIMS, Digitail's consolidation pitch is stronger than ours and this is not the ground to fight on.
They include unlimited staff users at no additional cost, so per-seat pricing is our weakest point on an account with sixteen locations of front-desk staff.
Their AI scribe is unreliable in exam rooms.

sections.title: Pivot points — what to say when they bring it up

sentences.text: If they say they are evaluating Digitail, agree first: if they want one system for records, invoicing and scheduling, Digitail is a serious option. Then move the question to what sixteen front desks would have to be retrained on.
If they say Digitail includes unlimited users, concede it plainly, then ask how many of those seats actually touch the calendar.

If they say they already have their own app, that is the strongest objection on this account — their members book in it and reviews name it — so position Thicket behind that app rather than in front of it.
If they ask what Digitail costs, say you do not know, because Digitail does not publish it. Refusing to guess is worth more than a number you cannot defend.
If they say they never overbook, that is their published promise, so the pitch is protecting that promise across sixteen sites rather than filling more slots.
Across your locations, who owns the appointment template — each clinic, or one person centrally?
Your site promises same or next-day appointments. How often do you actually hit that, and where does it break down?
You promise that appointments start on time. Do you measure it, and what does it look like on a bad Monday?
If you moved to a single all-in-one system, what would your team have to give up that they currently like?
Members book through your app. What happens today when someone calls instead?

price_comparisons.caveat: Digitail publishes no price for Growth — the plan routes to a demo. No per-seat comparison is possible without guessing.
Enterprise is quote-only ("Talk to sales"). Their unlimited-user model also means per-seat is the wrong unit for comparison.

feature_matrix.why: Small Door's brand promise is same or next-day availability, so booking is table stakes on this account rather than a differentiator.
Their comparison table lists SMS, MMS, two-way and mass texting as an add-on rather than a plan inclusion.
Listed on their page as an add-on. We do not offer it at all; unlikely to decide this deal.
Core to their all-in-one pitch and entirely outside our scope. Concede it early.

feature_matrix.feature: Unlimited staff users at no extra cost
feature_matrix.why: We charge per seat with a three-seat minimum. At sixteen locations this is our weakest commercial point.
Their stated value is eliminating multiple disconnected tools, which means replacing the incumbent rather than sitting next to it.
Small Door markets its own pricing transparency to pet owners, so an unquotable vendor is a values mismatch worth naming.
Complex schedule templates and room management ship in their Growth tier; ours are per-location and need central overrides.

feature_matrix.feature: No-show risk scoring on an appointment
feature_matrix.why: Nothing on their public pricing page mentions it. We say unknown rather than no — do not claim they lack it.

risk_flags.why: An exclusivity claim about a whole market is comparative advertising. We have not surveyed every scheduling vendor, and one counterexample on a live call destroys the rest of the card.
risk_flags.suggested_alternative: Thicket is one of the few scheduling tools that writes back to all three major veterinary PIMS.

risk_flags.why: A negative performance claim about a named competitor's product with no source behind it. This is the sentence most likely to be repeated on a call and the least defensible.
risk_flags.suggested_alternative: We have not seen independent benchmarks for their AI scribe — worth asking how it performs on your case mix.
